Part D · Chapter 6

Long context

What a longer text costs, and three ways to handle it

Attention compares a token with all earlier tokens, so its cost grows with the square of the length. This chapter counts that cost for the made-up SharkCam dive log, about 78,000 tokens as sentences, and follows three ways to handle it: sparse attention, a memory of fixed size, and test-time training, a memory trained while the model reads (In-Place TTT, which my MBZUAI project works on, adds it beside the cache).

You will need: attention and the causal mask (D4), the KV cache (D5), Big-O (0.2) and the outer product (0.5).

What a longer text costs

Guess first. In attention, one comparison of a token with an earlier token is a pair. If a text becomes twice as long, by what factor do the pairs grow, and by what factor does the rest of the work in a layer grow? For a long text, which is the larger part?

Under the causal mask a token is compared with itself and the tokens before it, so token \(i\) has \(i\) pairs, and a text of \(n\) tokens has \(1+2+\dots+n = n(n+1)/2\) pairs. This count is quadratic (Big-O, Part 0): it grows like \(n^2\), so doubling \(n\) multiplies it by about 4. The rest of a layer is the matrices that make queries, keys, values and outputs, and the MLP, a small network. They work on one token at a time, so their work doubles when \(n\) doubles. Because \(n^2\) grows faster than \(n\), attention is the larger part beyond some length.

  1. Coral is the work of attention pairs and navy the work of the rest of the layer. At the start (GPT-2 small sizes, 1,024 tokens) attention is 10.0% of the work.
  2. Press “dive log as text” (the made-up dive log as sentences, 78,163 GPT-2 tokens): attention rises to 89.4%.
  3. Choose “Qwen3-4B sizes”: the lines cross at about 24,639 tokens (the diamond), and at 78,163 tokens attention is 76.0%.

With GPT-2 small sizes, attention is 10% of a layer's work at 1,024 tokens and 89% at 78,163 GPT-2 tokens, and the lines cross at about 9,200 tokens.

How it works

Take GPT-2 small, a language model, at 1,024 tokens: its sizes include the attention width \(d_a = H\,d_{\text{head}} = 12 \times 64 = 768\) (heads times head size). A layer has \(P_{\text{block}} = 7{,}087{,}872\) weights and biases that act on one token at a time (\(4 \times 768^2\) in the projections, \(2 \times 768 \times 3{,}072\) in the MLP, and 9,984 biases and layer-norm values). The work of attention is \(1{,}024 \times 1{,}025 \times 768 = 806{,}092{,}800\) multiply-adds (one multiplication and one addition), and the work of the rest is \(1{,}024 \times 7{,}087{,}872 = 7{,}257{,}980{,}928\). So with both amounts in billions, attention is \(0.81 / (0.81 + 7.26) = 10\%\) of the layer's work.

\(T_{\text{att}}\)attention: 806,092,800=\(2d_a\)per pair: 1,536×\(n(n+1)/2\)pairs: 524,800and\(T_{\text{rest}}\)the rest: 7,257,980,928=\(n\)tokens: 1,024×\(P_{\text{block}}\)weights: 7,087,872

One pair takes \(2d_a\) multiply-adds. In one head a score (a dot product of vectors of \(d_{\text{head}}\) numbers) takes \(d_{\text{head}}\) multiply-adds and the weighted sum of value vectors takes \(d_{\text{head}}\) more, so \(H\) heads take \(2H\,d_{\text{head}} = 2d_a\). So the \(n(n+1)/2\) pairs take \(n(n+1)\,d_a\). The rest takes \(n\,P_{\text{block}}\), since a weight takes part in one multiply-add per token. Setting the two equal and dividing \(n(n+1)\,d_a = n\,P_{\text{block}}\) by \(n\,d_a\) gives \(n+1 = P_{\text{block}}/d_a\), so the lines cross at \(n^{*} = P_{\text{block}}/d_a - 1 = 9{,}228\).

Common belief. Attention is the slow part of a transformer, so for a longer text most of the work is always attention.

Why it fails. In GPT-2 small attention is a tenth of a layer at 1,024 tokens and 89% at 78,163 tokens, and it is the larger part only beyond \(n^{*} = 9{,}228\).

Better account. The weights dominate for short texts and the pairs for long texts, and the crossing length depends on the model (24,639 for Qwen3-4B).

Quick quiz

A text grows from 8,192 to 16,384 tokens. By what factors do the attention pairs and the rest of the layer's work grow?

The pairs grow by \(16{,}384 \times 16{,}385 / (8{,}192 \times 8{,}193) = 4.0\), and the rest by 2.

A made-up model has \(d_a = 2{,}048\) and \(P_{\text{block}} = 50{,}331{,}648\). At what length does attention take as much work as the rest of the layer?

\(n^{*} = P_{\text{block}}/d_a - 1 = 50{,}331{,}648 / 2{,}048 - 1 = 24{,}576 - 1 = 24{,}575\).

The finding at more lengths

With the sizes of GPT-2 small, attention is 10% of a layer's work at 1,024 tokens, 78% at 32,768 and 93% at 131,072. The lines cross at about 9,200 tokens here and at about 24,600 tokens for the sizes of Qwen3-4B.

The SharkCam lengths

A report is about 33 tokens in GPT-2's tokenizer. A logbook of 500 reports comes to about 16,400 tokens. The made-up dive log has 2,400 frames, one per second for 40 minutes. Written out as one sentence per frame ("At 313 s the camera was at 12.39 m, light 0.02473, ...") it is 211,412 characters. That is 78,163 GPT-2 tokens, or 109,699 tokens in the Qwen2.5 tokenizer, which cuts numbers into single digits (D1). As photos it is larger still. If a frame is a 224 by 224 photo cut into 16 by 16 patches (E1), a frame is 196 tokens and the dive is 470,400.

Where the two costs come from

The two lines count different things. The coral line counts attention pairs. For one pair the model computes a score, a dot product of two vectors of \(d_{\text{head}}\) numbers, and later a weighted sum that costs the same again. Over all heads, \(H\, d_{\text{head}} = d_a\), so one pair costs \(2 d_a\) multiply-adds. With the causal mask the pairs are \(1 + 2 + \dots + n = n(n+1)/2\). The navy line counts the rest of the layer: the matrices that make queries, keys, values and outputs, and the MLP. They work on one token at a time, so their cost is the number of tokens times the number of weights, \(P_{\text{block}}\).

\[ T_{\text{attention}} = 2\,d_a\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2} = n(n+1)\,d_a, \qquad T_{\text{rest}} = n\,P_{\text{block}}, \qquad n^{*} = \frac{P_{\text{block}}}{d_a} - 1 \]

  • \(n\) is the number of tokens. \(d_a\) is the width of the attention, the number of heads times the head size: 768 in GPT-2 small and 4,096 in Qwen3-4B (32 heads of 128).
  • \(P_{\text{block}}\) is the number of weights and biases in one block that act on one token at a time (attention projections and MLP). It is 7,087,872 in GPT-2 small (D5) and 100,925,440 in Qwen3-4B, computed from its configuration file.
  • \(n^{*}\) is the length at which the two costs are equal. Solve \(n(n+1)d_a = n\,P_{\text{block}}\) for \(n\).

The count includes only multiply-adds. The softmax of a row of scores needs one exponential per pair, which the count leaves out.

More worked examples

Worked example 1. GPT-2 small at \(n = 1{,}024\): attention costs \(1{,}024 \times 1{,}025 \times 768 = 806{,}092{,}800\) multiply-adds, and the rest costs \(1{,}024 \times 7{,}087{,}872 = 7{,}257{,}980{,}928\). Attention is \(0.81 / (0.81 + 7.26) = 10\%\) of the layer. Worked example 2. At \(n = 32{,}768\) attention costs 824.7 billion and the rest 232.3 billion, so attention is 78%. The crossing point is \(n^{*} = 7{,}087{,}872 / 768 - 1 = 9{,}228\). Vaswani and others (2017) list the same cost, \(O(n^2 d)\) per layer, in their Table 1, next to \(O(n d^2)\) for a recurrent layer. Attention is the cheaper of the two when \(n < d\).

Wider models, and writing one token

A wider model reaches the crossing point at a longer text. In a model built like GPT-2, \(P_{\text{block}}\) is about \(12d^2\) and \(d_a = d\), so \(n^{*}\) is about \(12d - 1\) and grows in proportion to the width \(d\). While a model writes, a new token is compared with the \(n\) tokens in the cache. That costs \(2n\,d_a\) multiply-adds, since a pair costs \(2d_a\) and there are \(n\) pairs, and it reads the whole cache from memory.

Memory

Memory has its own count. The attention matrix, the table of attention weights with one row per query token (D4), has \(n^2\) numbers per head and layer. At \(n = 32{,}768\) that is 1.07 billion numbers, or 2.1 GB in 16-bit numbers, for one head in one layer, and Qwen3-4B has 32 heads per layer. Programs avoid storing it. FlashAttention (Dao and others, 2022) computes the same result in tiles that stay in fast memory, so the full table is never written out. This lowers the memory and the traffic. The number of pairs stays the same, and so does the \(n^2\) in the time.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Count tokens, not words or characters. The dive log as sentences is 211,412 characters but 78,163 tokens. A Hindi report costs about five times as many tokens as its English meaning in GPT-2 (D1). The pairs grow with the square of the token count, so a language that costs five times the tokens costs about 25 times the pairs. The 117-token Hindi report has 6,903 kept scores under the causal mask of D4, against 276 for its 23-token English meaning.

In Python

def layer_cost(n, d_attn, w_block):
    attn = n * (n + 1) * d_attn          # score and weighted sum, allowed pairs only
    rest = n * w_block                   # projections and MLP: one pass per token
    return attn, rest

for name, d_attn, w_block in [("GPT-2 small", 768, 7_087_872), ("Qwen3-4B", 4096, 100_925_440)]:
    print(name, "attention equals the rest at n =", round(w_block / d_attn - 1))
    for n in (1_024, 8_192, 32_768, 131_072):
        a, r = layer_cost(n, d_attn, w_block)
        print(f"  n = {n:>7,}: attention is {a / (a + r):5.1%} of the layer")
n = 32_768
print("one head, 16-bit scores, n =", f"{n:,}:", f"{n * n * 2 / 1e9:.1f} GB if the whole matrix is stored")

More questions

Why does a wider model reach the crossing point at a longer text?

In a model built like GPT-2, \(n^{*} = P_{\text{block}} / d_a - 1\) has a numerator that grows like \(d^2\) and a denominator that grows like \(d\), so \(n^{*}\) grows with the width. GPT-2 small crosses at 9,228 tokens and Qwen3-4B at 24,639.

The key-value cache at actual sizes

Guess first. Qwen3-4B reads a report of 32,768 tokens, and its weights take about 8 GB in 16-bit numbers. Does the KV cache of the report take about 5 MB, about 5 GB or about 50 GB?

The key-value cache, or KV cache, stores the keys and values of the earlier tokens. A new token can then read them without computing them again (see the KV cache in the transformer chapter). It grows in proportion to the text length, so at some length it can exceed the weights of the model. Newer models store less by grouped-query attention (Ainslie and others, 2023). Several query heads, the usual attention heads, share one key-value head, the head whose keys and values are stored.

  1. The coral bar is the cache, the pale bar is the cache without sharing, and the navy bar is the weights. For Qwen3-4B at 32,768 tokens they are 4.8 GB, 19.3 GB and 8.0 GB.
  2. Choose “8-bit numbers”: the cache halves to 2.4 GB.
  3. Choose “16-bit numbers” again and drag the length slider towards 54,500 tokens: the coral bar grows until it is as long as the navy bar.

The cache of Qwen3-4B is 4.8 GB at 32,768 tokens and equals its weights (8.0 GB) at about 54,500 tokens, beyond its position limit of 40,960 tokens.

How it works

Take Qwen3-4B: 36 layers, 8 key-value heads, head size 128. One token needs \(2 \times 36 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 147{,}456\) bytes, so 32,768 tokens need \(147{,}456 \times 32{,}768 = 4{,}831{,}838{,}208\) bytes, or 4.8 GB. With 32 key-value heads, one per query head, the cache would be 19.3 GB, four times as large.

\(C\)cache: 4,831,838,208 bytes=2key and value×\(N_{\text{layer}}\)layers: 36×\(n_{kv}\)key-value heads: 8×\(d_{\text{head}}\)numbers per head: 128×\(b\)bytes per number: 2 (16-bit)×\(n\)tokens: 32,768

The cache stores a key and a value (the 2) per token, per layer, and per key-value head. So \(n_{kv} = 8\) enters the formula and the 32 query heads do not: queries are used once and are not stored. The function kv_bytes in the Go deeper part below computes this formula.

Common belief. A model with a context limit of 128,000 tokens reads 128,000 tokens as well as it reads 1,000.

Why it fails. The context limit, the most tokens that a model accepts, gives what fits, and the cache size gives what it costs, but neither measures how well the model uses the text. In tests by Liu and others (2023), models often answered best when the relevant passage was at the start or the end of a long input, and worse when it was in the middle.

Better account. Context limit, cache size and use are three numbers: the first two can be computed, and the third has to be tested on the task.

Quick quiz

Qwen2.5-0.5B has 24 layers and 2 key-value heads of size 64. How many bytes of cache does one token need in 16-bit numbers?

\(2 \times 24 \times 2 \times 64 \times 2 = 12{,}288\) bytes. For 32,768 tokens that is 403 MB.

Qwen3-4B has 32 query heads and 8 key-value heads. Which number enters the cache formula, and by what factor does it shrink the cache?

The number of key-value heads, \(n_{kv} = 8\), because the cache stores keys and values and not queries. It shrinks the cache by \(32 / 8 = 4\).

From the transformer chapter's formula to sharing

The formula in D5 was \(2 \times N_{\text{layer}} \times n \times d \times b\), and it assumed that all heads keep their own keys and values, as GPT-2 does. Newer models share. Qwen3-4B has 32 query heads but 8 key-value heads (its configuration file says num_key_value_heads: 8), so a group of 4 query heads reads one set of keys and values. Qwen2.5-0.5B has 14 query heads and 2 key-value heads. The cache therefore stores \(n_{kv}\) heads of size \(d_{\text{head}}\) per layer, and the pale bar in the figure shows what it would be without sharing.

The dotted line in the figure is the memory you chose with the second slider. Sizes come from the configuration files of the models and use 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes.

Symbols

\[ \text{cache size in bytes} = 2\times N_{\text{layer}}\times n_{kv}\times d_{\text{head}}\times n\times b \]

  • 2 is for keys and values. \(N_{\text{layer}}\) counts the layers that keep a key and a value for all tokens. \(n_{kv}\) is the number of key-value heads and \(d_{\text{head}}\) the numbers per head. \(n\) is the number of tokens and \(b\) the bytes per number (2 for 16-bit).
  • Without sharing, \(n_{kv} d_{\text{head}} = d\), the formula of D5.

More worked examples

Worked example 1. Qwen3-4B has 36 layers, 8 key-value heads and a head size of 128. For one token: \(2 \times 36 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 147{,}456\) bytes. For 32,768 tokens: \(147{,}456 \times 32{,}768 = 4{,}831{,}838{,}208\) bytes, or 4.8 GB. Without sharing it would have 32 key-value heads and the cache would be four times as large, 19.3 GB. Worked example 2. The SharkCam dive log written as sentences is 109,699 tokens in the Qwen2.5 tokenizer. Both configuration files give a vocabulary of 151,936, but this primer did not compare the two tokenizers, so take the count as an estimate for Qwen3. Its cache in Qwen3-4B's sizes would be \(147{,}456 \times 109{,}699 = 16.2\) GB, twice the weights. The configuration file gives Qwen3-4B a position limit of 40,960 tokens, so a text this long also needs position scaling (D5).

A model with linear layers

Select the last model, Qwen3.6-27B. Its configuration file lists 64 layers, of which 16 are labelled full_attention and 48 linear_attention. Only the 16 keep keys and values for all tokens. The other 48 keep a state of fixed size, which the next sections explain. The figure adds an estimate of that state: a 128 by 128 matrix for 48 value heads in 48 layers, read from the configuration (the model's code was not read). It is small next to the growing cache.

Making the cache smaller

A bigger cache also makes the model slower, because a decoding step reads the whole cache from memory to attend over it. Practitioners shrink the cache in four ways. They share keys and values (grouped-query attention). They store them in 8-bit numbers, which halves the cache, and the effect on answers has to be measured per model. They drop old tokens (the next sections). They use fewer full layers (the hybrid model above).

The position of the passage in a long input

Liu and others (2023) found the same drop in the middle (see the common belief above) for models built for long contexts.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. To estimate a cache, read num_key_value_heads in the configuration, not num_attention_heads. For Qwen3-4B the wrong one overestimates the cache four times.

In Python

def kv_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, n, bytes_per_number=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * n * bytes_per_number

# Qwen3-4B from its configuration file: 36 layers, 32 query heads, 8 key-value heads, head size 128
for n in (4_096, 32_768, 131_072):
    shared = kv_bytes(36, 8, 128, n)
    own = kv_bytes(36, 32, 128, n)
    print(f"n = {n:>7,}: cache {shared / 1e9:5.1f} GB, without sharing {own / 1e9:5.1f} GB")
weights = 4.02e9 * 2
tokens = (16e9 - weights) / kv_bytes(36, 8, 128, 1)
print(f"16 GB of memory: {weights / 1e9:.1f} GB for the weights leaves space for {tokens:,.0f} tokens")
dive = 109_699   # the made-up dive log as sentences, Qwen2.5 tokenizer
print(f"dive log as text, {dive:,} tokens: {kv_bytes(36, 8, 128, dive) / 1e9:.1f} GB")

n =  32,768: cache   4.8 GB, without sharing  19.3 GB
n = 131,072: cache  19.3 GB, without sharing  77.3 GB

More questions

Why does the cache of the hybrid model grow more slowly than that of a 64-layer model with full attention in all layers?

Only 16 of its 64 layers keep keys and values for all tokens. The other 48 keep a state whose size does not depend on \(n\).

Looking at fewer pairs

Guess first. For 64 tokens, causal attention computes \(64 \times 65 / 2 = 2{,}080\) pairs, and if a token may look only at the last 8 tokens (itself included), about what share of the pairs remains? Which few extra pairs would you add so that a token can still reach far?

Sparse attention needs only the pairs that a mask keeps, and a program saves time only if it skips the others. In a sliding window of \(w\) tokens, a token looks only at itself and the \(w-1\) tokens before it. A few extra pairs let information reach far. Global tokens are looked at by all tokens. A stride \(l\) adds the tokens \(l\), \(2l\), \(3l\), ... places before the token that looks. Random keys are a few other tokens chosen at random for that token. With such a mask the pairs grow in proportion to \(n\), or to \(n\sqrt{n}\) for a stride near \(\sqrt{n}\), instead of \(n^2\).

  1. Rows are the tokens that look, columns the tokens looked at, and a coloured cell is a computed pair. The window (\(w = 8\)) computes 484 of the 2,080 pairs of 64 tokens, 23.3%.
  2. Raise Tokens n to 96: the band keeps its width and the share kept falls to 15.9%.
  3. Press “Strided”, then “Stride = square root of n”: the growth from 10,000 to 20,000 tokens in the line under the chart falls from ×3.98 to ×2.83 (full mask: ×4.00).

A window of 8 keeps 484 of 2,080 pairs (23.3%), and doubling the length about doubles the window's pairs but about quadruples the full count.

How it works

Take 64 tokens and a window of \(w = 8\). The first 8 rows have 1, 2, ..., 8 keys, which add up to 36, and the other 56 rows have 8 keys, which add up to 448. So the total is \(36 + 448 = 484\) pairs, against 2,080 for causal attention.

\(\text{pairs}\)of the window: 484=\(w\)window width: 8×\(n\)tokens: 64−\(w(w-1)/2\)missing at the start: 28

If all \(n\) rows had \(w\) keys, the total would be \(w\,n\). The first \(w-1\) rows have fewer, because row \(i\) has only \(i\) keys, and the gaps \((w-1) + (w-2) + \dots + 1\) add up to \(w(w-1)/2\). So the window's pairs grow in proportion to \(n\), while the full count grows like \(n^2/2\). The code in the Go deeper part below counts the pairs of the patterns.

Common belief. Sparse attention is the same model with a cheaper calculation.

Why it fails. It changes what a token can read, so a model trained with full attention gives different answers when pairs are removed, as cutting a trained model's attention shows. Longformer, the Sparse Transformer and BigBird, three published models that use such patterns, are trained with their patterns.

Better account. A sparse pattern is a design choice that trades some reach for a cost that grows more slowly, and models like these are trained with it.

Quick quiz

A causal window of 4 over 10 tokens: how many pairs, and what share of the 55 pairs of causal attention?

\(4 \times 10 - 4 \times 3 / 2 = 34\) pairs, which is 62%. Rows 1 to 4 have 1, 2, 3 and 4 keys, and the other 6 rows have 4: \(10 + 24 = 34\).

A causal window of 64 and 2 global tokens at the start of the text: how many keys does token 1,000 look at?

The window gives 64 keys, and the 2 global tokens, which lie outside the window, give 2 more: 66.

Go deeper the four patterns, derivation, examples, Python about 6 min

Reading the figure

A row of the grid is one query token and a column is one key token. A filled cell is a pair that is computed. Start with the sliding window and raise \(n\). The filled band stays as wide as \(w\), so the line in the chart grows in step with \(n\) and leaves the full line behind. Then try the others.

With a window, the work per token stops growing with the length. The chart is log-log, so a pattern whose line is parallel to the full line still has a square in it.

The four patterns

  • Sliding window. Longformer (Beltagy and others, 2020) gives a token a fixed window of \(w\) tokens, \(w/2\) on both sides, and the cost is \(O(n \times w)\). In the left-to-right version the window is the last \(w\) tokens, the token itself included.
  • Strided. The Sparse Transformer (Child and others, 2019) uses two kinds of head: one looks at the previous \(l\) places and one at the places \(l\), \(2l\), \(3l\), ... back. The figure shows both together. With \(l\) near \(\sqrt{n}\) the total is \(O(n\sqrt{n})\), and any two tokens are joined in two steps. Switch the stride to the square root of \(n\) and watch the slope of the line in the chart. The authors found that a strided pattern works well for data with a natural stride, such as images, and that for text a fixed pattern works better.
  • Global + window. A few tokens, such as the classification token of an encoder, look at all tokens and are seen by all. Longformer chooses them for the task. When tokens read only the past, a global token at the start is seen by all later tokens and sees no earlier token. Cutting a trained model's attention shows why this still matters.
  • Random + window + global. BigBird (Zaheer and others, 2020) adds \(r\) random keys per query. Random links shorten the paths between tokens, as they do in a random graph. In their experiments at length 512 (Table 1 of the paper), random keys alone and a window alone were both worse than full attention at predicting masked words (scores of 60.1 and 58.3 against 64.2). The two together were better than either (62.7), and global tokens were the final piece.

Counting the pairs of a window

The count for a window follows from adding up the rows. Row \(i\) of the causal window has \(i\) keys while \(i \le w\), and \(w\) keys after that. So the first \(w\) rows add up to \(w(w+1)/2\), and the other \(n - w\) rows to \((n-w)w\):

\[ \text{pairs}(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \min(i, w) = \frac{w(w+1)}{2} + (n-w)\,w = w\,n - \frac{w(w-1)}{2} \]

  • \(n\) is the number of tokens and \(w\) the window width. When \(w \ge n\) the window is the whole causal mask and the count is \(n(n+1)/2\).
  • For a window read both ways with \(h = \lfloor w/2 \rfloor\) tokens on both sides the count is \((2h+1)\,n - h(h+1)\).

More worked examples

Worked example 1. Take \(n = 2{,}400\) (the frames of the dive, if a frame were one token) and \(w = 64\). The window computes \(64 \times 2{,}400 - 64 \times 63 / 2 = 153{,}600 - 2{,}016 = 151{,}584\) pairs. Causal attention computes \(2{,}400 \times 2{,}401 / 2 = 2{,}881{,}200\), so the window keeps 5.3%. Worked example 2. Take the dive log as sentences, \(n = 78{,}163\) GPT-2 tokens, with \(w = 4{,}096\). The window computes \(4{,}096 \times 78{,}163 - 4{,}096 \times 4{,}095 / 2 = 311{,}769{,}088\) pairs, against 3,054,766,366 for causal attention. That is 10.2%. Doubling the log to 156,326 tokens about doubles the window's pairs (to about 630 million) and quadruples the full count.

Worked example 3. For 4,096 tokens causal attention computes 8,390,656 pairs. A window of 64 computes \(64 \times 4{,}096 - 64 \times 63 / 2 = 262{,}144 - 2{,}016 = 260{,}128\) pairs, which is 3.1%.

Where the pattern works, where it breaks, and speed

This pattern works when most of what a token needs is near it, and when a few tokens pass summaries on to the rest. It breaks when an answer depends on a detail far away that no global, strided or random link reaches. One practical point: the skipped pairs only save time if the code skips them. A mask applied to a full \(n \times n\) table, as in the code below, computes all the pairs first. Child and others and Beltagy and others wrote special GPU programs for their patterns for this reason.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Draw the mask for a small \(n\) before you trust it, as in D4, and check the number of keys in the first rows. The common slip is one place too many or too few: does the window include the token itself? In the code below, token 11 with a window of 4 reads tokens 8, 9, 10 and 11.

In Python

import numpy as np

def masks(n, w, l, g):
    i = np.arange(n)[:, None]; j = np.arange(n)[None, :]
    causal = j <= i
    window = causal & (j > i - w)                          # the last w tokens, itself included
    strided = causal & ((i - j <= l) | ((i - j) % l == 0)) # the last l tokens and the tokens l, 2l, 3l, ... back
    global_window = window | (causal & (j < g))            # window plus g global tokens at the start
    return {"full": np.ones((n, n), bool), "causal": causal, "window": window,
            "strided": strided, "global + window": global_window}

n, w, g = 2400, 64, 2
l = round(n ** 0.5)
for name, m in masks(n, w, l, g).items():
    print(f"{name:16s} {m.sum():>9,} pairs  {m.sum() / n**2:6.1%} of n x n")
print("formula for the window:", w * n - w * (w - 1) // 2)
full             5,760,000 pairs  100.0% of n x n
causal           2,881,200 pairs   50.0% of n x n
window             151,584 pairs    2.6% of n x n
strided            174,000 pairs    3.0% of n x n
global + window    156,255 pairs    2.7% of n x n
formula for the window: 151584
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
n, d = 12, 4
q, k, v = rng.normal(size=(3, n, d))

def attention(q, k, v, mask):
    s = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(d)
    s = np.where(mask, s, -np.inf)                 # skipped pairs get weight 0
    w = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True))
    w /= w.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    return w @ v

i = np.arange(n)[:, None]; j = np.arange(n)[None, :]
window = (j <= i) & (j > i - 4)                    # the last 4 tokens
out = attention(q, k, v, window)

# the same thing as a loop that only ever touches the 4 allowed keys
loop = np.zeros_like(v)
for t in range(n):
    keys = range(max(0, t - 3), t + 1)
    s = np.array([q[t] @ k[u] / np.sqrt(d) for u in keys])
    w = np.exp(s - s.max()); w /= w.sum()
    loop[t] = sum(w[a] * v[u] for a, u in enumerate(keys))
print("pairs in the mask:", window.sum(), "of", n * (n + 1) // 2)
print("largest difference between mask and loop:", np.abs(out - loop).max())
print("token 11 reads tokens", np.flatnonzero(window[11]))
pairs in the mask: 42 of 78
largest difference between mask and loop: 2.220446049250313e-16
token 11 reads tokens [ 8  9 10 11]

More questions

Why does the stride in the Sparse Transformer grow like \(\sqrt{n}\)?

A row has about \(l\) keys from the window part and about \(n/l\) from the stride part. The sum \(l + n/l\) is smallest when \(l \approx \sqrt{n}\), where a row has about \(2\sqrt{n}\) keys and the total is \(O(n\sqrt{n})\).

How far information travels

Guess first. A model has a causal window of 3 tokens: a token reads itself and the two before it. Can token 25 in the top layer depend on token 1, and if it can, how many layers does that take?

A layer is one round of attention and MLP (the transformer block), and layers are stacked, so a token can use the outputs of tokens that attended to others in the layer before. The input tokens that can influence one output are its receptive field. A causal window of \(w\) tokens widens it by \(w-1\) places per layer, so after \(L\) layers a token can receive information from up to \(L(w-1)\) places back. A global token, which reads all tokens and is read by all, shortens the path. If tokens read both ways, looking at later tokens as well as earlier ones, two layers are enough.

  1. Teal dots mark the tokens that can influence the coral token at the top. With the window \(w = 3\) reading the past and \(L = 3\) layers, 7 tokens reach token 25: the reach grows by 2 places per layer.
  2. Drag Layers L to 8: 17 tokens reach token 25, back to token 9, and the readout says 12 layers are needed to reach token 1.
  3. Press “Window + global token, both ways” and set L to 2: all 25 input tokens are teal.

With a causal window of 3, token 25 needs 12 layers to receive information from token 1. With one global token and tokens reading both ways, 2 layers are enough.

How it works

Follow token 25 down the stack with \(w = 3\): in the top layer it reads tokens 23 to 25 of the layer below. These read tokens 21 to 25 of the layer under that, so the reach grows by 2 places per layer. After 12 layers it is \(12 \times 2 = 24\) places, which reaches token 1 (\(25 - 24\)). With a global token read both ways, the global token reads all tokens in layer 1 and token 25 reads the global token in layer 2.

\(L(w-1)\)places back: 24=\(L\)layers: 12×\(w-1\)places per layer: 2

The factor \(w-1\) is there because a window of \(w\) tokens contains the token itself and \(w-1\) earlier tokens. The formula gives an upper bound on where information can come from. How much of it arrives has to be measured, because it goes through many layers.

Common belief. If the window is shorter than the text, the model cannot connect tokens that are far apart.

Why it fails. Layers pass information on. A token that cannot see token 1 directly can use the output of a token that attended to it.

Better account. Stacked windows reach up to \(L(w-1)\) places, but information passed on through layers is mixed with that of other tokens. A global token gives a direct route.

Quick quiz

A causal window of 5 and 8 layers: how far back can the top token get information from?

\(8 \times (5-1) = 32\) places back, so the receptive field is 33 tokens.

Why does one global token, with tokens reading both ways, let any token reach any other in 2 layers?

In layer 1 the global token reads all tokens. In layer 2 all tokens read the global token, which now contains a summary of all of them.

Go deeper reading the figure, other patterns, a debug tip about 2 min

Reading the figure

Read the figure from the top. The coral token at layer \(L\) reads a few tokens of layer \(L-1\), and those tokens read a few tokens of layer \(L-2\). The teal set is the receptive field. For a causal window of width \(w\) it grows by \(w - 1\) places per layer. Stacked windows widen the reach like the stacked filters of a convolutional network. So token 25 reaches token 1 after \(\lceil 24 / 2 \rceil = 12\) layers. Longformer states the rule for a window that reads both ways: the top layer of an \(l\)-layer model with window \(w\) has a receptive field of about \(l \times w\), as in convolutional networks. A dilated window, one with gaps, grows faster (Beltagy and others, 2020).

Other patterns, and the reach of Qwen3-4B

The other patterns cut the path. With a global token read both ways, the global token reads all tokens in layer 1, and token 25 reads the global token in layer 2, so token 25 has seen all tokens after 2 layers. The Sparse Transformer was designed for the same property. Any position reaches any other in a small constant number of steps (two, for its two-dimensional patterns), which is why a stride near \(\sqrt{n}\) is used. Worked example. Qwen3-4B has 36 layers and uses full attention. If it used a causal window of 4,096 tokens, information could come from at most \(36 \times 4{,}095 = 147{,}420\) places back. That is an upper bound on where information can come from. How much of it arrives is a question for measurement, because it has to be relayed through 36 layers.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. When you choose a window, compute the reach \(L(w-1)\) first and compare it with the distance between a question and the facts it needs. If the reach is shorter, no choice of weights will connect them.

Cutting a trained model's attention

Guess first. GPT-2 small was trained to see all earlier tokens. At test time, with no retraining, we give it a window of 128: a token sees only itself and the 127 tokens before it. Its loss on tokens 513 to 1,024 of a made-up logbook is 1.7 nats per token. Will the loss rise to about 2, about 4 or about 8?

The loss is the average of \(-\ln p\) over the tokens, where \(p\) is the probability that the model gave to the actual next token. Its unit is the nat (see the loss in the next-token chapter). We cut a trained model's attention by setting the scores outside a pattern to minus infinity before the softmax, so those pairs get attention weight 0. With a window alone the loss rises sharply, and it rises much less when the first token also stays visible.

  1. Choose “Window only” and set the window to 128: the loss (navy line) is 7.84, against 1.69 for full attention (dotted line).
  2. Choose “Window + first token”: at 128 the loss is 2.58. The grid shades the 144 heads (12 layers with 12 heads in a layer) by the share of their attention weight inside the pattern, and the mean of these 144 shares rises from 50% to 80%.

From 1.69 nats per token with full attention, a window of 128 raises the loss of GPT-2 small to 7.84, and to 2.58 when the first token also stays visible.

How it works

Compare two cuts at a window of 128: the window alone computes \(128 \times 1{,}024 - 128 \times 127/2 = 131{,}072 - 8{,}128 = 122{,}944\) pairs (23.4% of 524,800) and has loss 7.84. Adding the first token as a key for the \(1{,}024 - 128 = 896\) tokens whose window lacks it gives 123,840 pairs (23.6%) and loss 2.58.

\(\text{pairs}\)with first token: 123,840=\(wn - w(w-1)/2\)window: 122,944+\(n-w\)first token: 896

The 896 extra pairs are 0.17% of the 524,800. Yet in full attention, averaged over tokens 513 to 1,024, 31 of the 144 heads give the first token over half of their attention weight. Xiao and others (2023) call such a token an attention sink and suggest that heads put weight on it when no other token matches their query. Without it, the softmax spreads that weight over other tokens and changes the output of these heads, a likely reason for the rise in loss.

Common belief. A sliding window only drops old tokens that matter little, so cutting it costs little.

Why it fails. The oldest token matters here: at a window of 128, dropping it raises the loss from 2.58 to 7.84.

Better account. Keep a few first tokens beside the window (the figure keeps one), or train the model with the pattern, and measure on your own text. This test used one model and one text, so a difference of 0.018 nats could shrink or reverse on another text.

Quick quiz

In the figure, which line is higher at a window of 64, window only or window plus first token? Why?

Window only (8.66 against 2.94). A likely reason: with the first token visible, the weight that many heads give it stays available to them.

With a window of 512 and the first token the loss is 1.675, and with full attention it is 1.693. Does this show that the cut model is better?

No. The difference is 0.018 nats, which could shrink or reverse on a different text, and the test used one model and one text.

Go deeper test details, the saving, a debug tip about 3 min

How the test was run

The test used GPT-2 small (D3) on a logbook of 1,024 tokens. The logbook has three parts. First come the 16 invented reports, in English, with the English meaning used for the Hindi, Marathi and Hinglish ones. Then come the 10 events of the made-up dive log, and then lines of the log itself. Before the softmax, all pairs outside the pattern were set to minus infinity (D4). The loss was measured on the second half of the logbook, tokens 513 to 1,024. No weights were retrained. The grid shows, for the 144 heads, how much of its attention weight lies inside the window, averaged over the same tokens.

Reading the figure

Press Window only and drag the window down. The loss climbs from 3.19 at 512 tokens to 7.84 at 128 and 16.75 at one token. Now press Window + first token. At 128 tokens the loss is 2.58 instead. The grid shows how much of a head's weight the pattern keeps. Many heads send much of their weight to the first token: 31 of the 144 put more than half of their weight on it, and the mean is 30%. D4 found this for another text. Xiao and others (2023) named it the attention sink and suggest that it is a resting place for heads that have no token to look up. In a window that drops the first token, the softmax spreads this weight over the other tokens, a likely reason for the rise in loss. Keeping the first token restores most of the performance of window attention (Xiao and others, 2023).

How much the cut saves

The saving is modest for this model. A window of 256 plus the first token computes 230,272 pairs, 43.9% of the 524,800 of causal attention, and the loss is 1.99, 0.30 nats above full attention. A window of 512 plus the first token computes 393,984 pairs (75.1%) at about the full-attention loss. Click the head L5H5 in the grid, the induction head of D4. A window of 64 keeps only 33% of its weight, and 54% with the first token. The head looks back to an earlier copy of a token, which may be far away. A task that needs the far copy loses it.

Reading the result with care

Read the result with care. It is one model, one text of 1,024 tokens, and the logbook is repetitive. A difference of 0.018 nats between 1.675 and 1.693 on one text could shrink or reverse on a different text. A model trained with its window from the start, as Longformer and the Sparse Transformer are, can learn to work inside it.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a model works at short lengths and produces strange text once its cache is trimmed to a window, check whether the first tokens were dropped. Compare the loss with and without them, as in the figure.

More questions

Why is the induction head L5H5 hurt more by a short window than most heads?

It attends to the token after an earlier copy of the current token. Copies can be far back, outside a short window.

A memory of fixed size

Guess first. The cache stores two vectors per token. Could one table of numbers of a fixed size, updated as a token arrives, replace it? How many items could a table of 16 by 16 numbers store, and what happens to the 17th?

Without the softmax (linear attention), the output of a token, a sum over earlier tokens of score times value, can be written as one matrix \(S\), the state. A new token updates \(S\) by adding the outer product \(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{k}^\top\) of its value and key (outer product, Part 0). The memory then stops growing, and what it can store is limited by its size. The delta rule adds only the difference between a new value \(\mathbf{v}\) and what \(S\) returns for the key: \(\eta\,(\mathbf{v} - S\mathbf{k})\,\mathbf{k}^\top\), where \(\eta\) is a step size. A state-space model also keeps a state of fixed size.

  1. Made-up keys and values: a bar is the error when a stored item (a key with its value) is read back. Drag Items stored n to 16 and all bars are zero, because the figure makes the first 16 keys at right angles to one another, which a trained model does not do. At 17 the bars rise, also for earlier items.
  2. Set n to 20 and choose “Window of 4”: only the last 4 items read back well, with error under 0.25 (4 of 20).
  3. Choose “Delta rule (test-time training)”: the newest item has error 0.00, and item 1 has error 0.61.

A 16 by 16 matrix reads back up to 16 well-separated items without error; a window of 4 cannot read older ones; the delta rule keeps the newest item right.

How it works

Take made-up items with two-number keys and values: key \((1,0)\) with value \((3,1)\), and key \((0,1)\) with value \((-1,2)\). Their outer products add up to \(S = \begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), and the first key reads back \(S\mathbf{k} = (3,1)\), the stored value, since the keys are at right angles. A third item, key \((0.6,0.8)\) with value \((5,-4)\), overlaps both: it adds \(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{k}^\top = \begin{pmatrix}5\times0.6&5\times0.8\\-4\times0.6&-4\times0.8\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3&4\\-2.4&-3.2\end{pmatrix}\), so \(S\) becomes \(\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}3&4\\-2.4&-3.2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}6&3\\-1.4&-1.2\end{pmatrix}\), and the first key now reads back \(S\mathbf{k} = (6,-1.4)\), the first column of \(S\).

\(S_i\)state after item i=\(S_{i-1}\)state before+\(\mathbf{v}_i\mathbf{k}_i^\top\)outer product;\(S\mathbf{k}_i\)read item i=\(\mathbf{v}_i\)stored value+\(\sum_{j\ne i}(\mathbf{k}_j\!\cdot\!\mathbf{k}_i)\,\mathbf{v}_j\)noise from other items

The sum can be written as one matrix because a score without the softmax is \(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}\) and \((\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k})\,\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\mathbf{k}^\top\mathbf{q}\), so the output for a query \(\mathbf{q}\) is \(\sum_j (\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}_j)\,\mathbf{v}_j = \bigl(\sum_j \mathbf{v}_j\mathbf{k}_j^\top\bigr)\mathbf{q} = S\mathbf{q}\). Here the keys have length 1. The noise is zero when all other keys are at right angles to \(\mathbf{k}_i\), which means \(\mathbf{k}_j\cdot\mathbf{k}_i = 0\). A key of 16 numbers allows at most 16 such directions, so a 17th key adds noise.

Common belief. A memory of fixed size can remember a long text as well as a cache does.

Why it fails. A cache of 100,000 tokens stores 100,000 separate keys and values. A matrix can read back only about as many items without noise as a key has numbers, however it is trained.

Better account. A fixed memory trades full recall for a cost that does not grow, and a cache is safer for a detail far back.

Quick quiz

A head has keys and values of 128 numbers. How many numbers does its state have, and how many a cache of 10,000 tokens?

The state has \(128 \times 128 = 16{,}384\) numbers whatever the length. The cache has \(2 \times 10{,}000 \times 128 = 2{,}560{,}000\) numbers. The state is smaller from about 64 tokens on.

Why can the sum memory read back 16 items without error but not 17?

Reading item \(i\) gives \(\mathbf{v}_i\) plus noise \(\sum_{j\ne i} (\mathbf{k}_j\cdot\mathbf{k}_i)\mathbf{v}_j\). The noise is zero when all other keys are at right angles to \(\mathbf{k}_i\). A vector of 16 numbers has at most 16 directions at right angles, so the 17th key cannot be at right angles to all the others.

Go deeper derivations, decay, state-space models, limits, Python about 7 min

Reading the figure

The keys and values are made up. The first 16 keys are orthonormal and later keys are random unit vectors.

Press Reset and then Play with the sum memory chosen (Play continues from the number of items already stored). While 16 or fewer items are stored, all bars are zero. Item 17 cannot have a key of its own, because a vector of 16 numbers has space for only 16 directions at right angles. From then on the bars rise, also for the items stored before. Now choose the others. The full cache stays accurate at any length, but it stores \(2 \times n \times 16\) numbers and so grows. The window keeps 128 numbers and cannot read items older than 4. The decay memory loses the older items gradually.

Where the matrix comes from

Where does the matrix come from? Take softmax-free attention for token \(i\), with a score \(\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{k}_j\) and no softmax. The output is \(\sum_{j \le i} (\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{k}_j)\,\mathbf{v}_j\). The number \(\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{k}_j\) multiplies the vector \(\mathbf{v}_j\), and \((\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k})\,\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\,\mathbf{k}^\top \mathbf{q}\). So the query can be pulled out of the sum:

\[ \mathbf{o}_i = \sum_{j\le i}\mathbf{v}_j\,\mathbf{k}_j^\top\,\mathbf{q}_i = S_i\,\mathbf{q}_i,\qquad S_i = S_{i-1} + \mathbf{v}_i\mathbf{k}_i^\top \]

  • \(S_i\) is the state after token \(i\): a matrix with one row per number in a value and one column per number in a key. It is the sum of the outer products of all earlier pairs.
  • Cost. One update and one read take about \(d_v d_k\) multiply-adds, whatever \(i\) is. So the total is \(O(n\,d^2)\) against \(O(n^2 d)\), and the memory is \(d_v d_k\) numbers whatever \(n\) is. Katharopoulos and others (2020) add a feature map to the queries and keys and a normaliser, and show that this form is a recurrent network.

Reading an item back

Reading item \(i\) back with its own key gives the value plus noise from the others:

\[ S\,\mathbf{k}_i = \mathbf{v}_i + \sum_{j\ne i}(\mathbf{k}_j\!\cdot\!\mathbf{k}_i)\,\mathbf{v}_j \]

  • The sum is zero when all keys are at right angles to \(\mathbf{k}_i\), so \(d\) items can be separated. For random unit keys in \(d\) numbers the noise has a typical size of \(\sqrt{(n-1)/d}\).

A worked example in two dimensions

Worked example with made-up numbers in two dimensions. Items: key \((1,0)\) with value \((3,1)\), key \((0,1)\) with value \((-1,2)\), key \((0.6,0.8)\) with value \((5,-4)\). After the first two items, \(S = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\). Reading with the first key gives \((3,1)\), the stored value, because the keys are at right angles. The third key overlaps both. After it, \(S = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 3\\ -1.4 & -1.2\end{pmatrix}\). Reading with the first key now gives \((6, -1.4)\) instead of \((3, 1)\), and with the third key \((6, -1.8)\) instead of \((5, -4)\). The third key has overlaps of 0.6 and 0.8 with the others, and so picks up \(0.6 \times (3,1) + 0.8 \times (-1,2) = (1, 2.2)\).

The delta rule

The delta rule fixes some of this. Before writing a pair, read what the matrix already predicts for the key, and write only the difference, scaled by a step size \(\eta\):

\[ S \leftarrow S + \eta\,(\mathbf{v} - S\mathbf{k})\,\mathbf{k}^\top \]

  • With \(\eta = 1\) and a key of length 1, the matrix returns \(\mathbf{v}\) for this key straight after the write. The correction is the gradient step of the next section.

In the example, the third write stores the difference \((5,-4) - S(0.6,0.8) = (5,-4) - (1,2.2) = (4,-6.2)\). Reading with the third key then gives \((5,-4)\), the stored value. Reading with the first key gives \((5.4, -2.72)\), worse than before for the first item. The delta rule makes the newest item right and pays for it with older items that overlap.

State-space models

The state-space family has the same plan with a different update. A state-space model keeps a state \(\mathbf{h}\) and updates it as \(\mathbf{h}_t = A\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + B x_t\), with a read-out \(y_t = C\mathbf{h}_t\). S4 (Gu, Goel and Ré, 2021) made this fast and good at long ranges. Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) lets the step size, \(B\) and \(C\) depend on the current token, so what the state keeps and forgets depends on the current token. Its authors report linear scaling in the sequence length and about five times the throughput of transformers at inference. The decay memory in the figure, \(S \leftarrow \gamma S + \mathbf{v}\mathbf{k}^\top\), is the simplest form of such a forget factor.

The limit of a fixed state

The counting sets the limit. A matrix of \(d_{\text{head}}^2\) numbers can separate about \(d_{\text{head}}\) items. A head of size 128 can keep about 128 items apart however long the text is, so what it keeps of a text of 100,000 tokens is a summary. A fixed memory works for tasks where a summary is enough, and a cache is safer for a detail far back. This may be one reason why some recent models mix the two kinds of layer. The configuration of Qwen3.6-27B has 48 linear layers and 16 full-attention layers, in blocks of three linear layers and one full layer. Its model card calls the linear layers Gated DeltaNet, a layer that combines a decay with the delta rule of this section (Yang and others, 2024). The reasons the authors chose this mix are in their own documentation, which this primer did not read.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a model with a linear or state-space layer loses a detail from far back, check the task before the code. Looking up one planted item by its key is the hardest test for a fixed memory, and averages over long texts hide it.

In Python

import numpy as np

k = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [0.6, 0.8]])      # keys of three items
v = np.array([[3.0, 1.0], [-1.0, 2.0], [5.0, -4.0]])    # their values

def write_sum(S, key, val):
    return S + np.outer(val, key)                        # linear attention: add v k^T

def write_delta(S, key, val, eta=1.0):
    return S + eta * np.outer(val - S @ key, key)        # store only what S gets wrong

for name, write in (("sum", write_sum), ("delta", write_delta)):
    S = np.zeros((2, 2))
    for key, val in zip(k, v):
        S = write(S, key, val)
    print(name, "matrix:\n", S.round(2))
    for i in range(3):
        print(f"  read item {i + 1}: {(S @ k[i]).round(2)}  stored {v[i]}")
sum matrix:
 [[ 6.   3. ]
 [-1.4 -1.2]]
  read item 1: [ 6.  -1.4]  stored [3. 1.]
  read item 2: [ 3.  -1.2]  stored [-1.  2.]
  read item 3: [ 6.  -1.8]  stored [ 5. -4.]
delta matrix:
 [[ 5.4   2.2 ]
 [-2.72 -2.96]]
  read item 1: [ 5.4  -2.72]  stored [3. 1.]
  read item 2: [ 2.2  -2.96]  stored [-1.  2.]
  read item 3: [ 5. -4.]  stored [ 5. -4.]
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = 16

def recall_error(n, rule):
    # first d keys are orthonormal, later ones random unit vectors
    Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(d, d)))
    keys = [Q[:, i] for i in range(min(n, d))]
    for _ in range(max(0, n - d)):
        x = rng.normal(size=d); keys.append(x / np.linalg.norm(x))
    vals = [(lambda x: x / np.linalg.norm(x))(rng.normal(size=d)) for _ in range(n)]
    S = np.zeros((d, d))
    for key, val in zip(keys, vals):
        S = S + np.outer(val, key) if rule == "sum" else S + np.outer(val - S @ key, key)
    return np.array([np.linalg.norm(S @ key - val) for key, val in zip(keys, vals)])

for n in (8, 16, 20, 24):
    e_sum, e_delta = recall_error(n, "sum"), recall_error(n, "delta")
    print(f"n = {n:2d}: oldest item error  sum {e_sum[0]:.2f}  delta {e_delta[0]:.2f};  newest item  sum {e_sum[-1]:.2f}  delta {e_delta[-1]:.2f}")

n = 16: oldest item error  sum 0.00  delta 0.00;  newest item  sum 0.00  delta 0.00
n = 20: oldest item error  sum 0.66  delta 0.60;  newest item  sum 1.14  delta 0.00
n = 24: oldest item error  sum 0.79  delta 0.67;  newest item  sum 0.88  delta 0.00

Learning the memory while reading

Guess first. The update of the matrix in the last section is a fixed rule. What if the update were a gradient step, as in training, on a loss computed from the text itself? Which weights would the step change, and when would you take it?

Test-time training updates some weights while the model reads, with a loss made from the input. Here the updated weights form a memory matrix \(W\), a small model. \(W\) is a fast weight: it changes while the model reads, and the other weights stay as trained. After a chunk (a block of tokens) has been read, one gradient step on a loss updates \(W\). The target of that loss is made from the chunk itself, so no labels are needed. For the next input \(W\) starts again from its trained value.

  1. Press “Read next chunk” twice (made-up keys and values). With squared error (the loss \(\tfrac12\lVert W\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{v}\rVert^2\)) and step size \(\eta = 1\) the loss on a chunk falls from 2.00 to 0.00, and all 8 tokens read so far read back well.
  2. Press Reset, choose “Chunks read twice” and read one chunk with squared error: 4 of 4 tokens read back well. Then choose “Dot product (In-Place TTT)”, whose loss \(-\mathbf{v}\cdot(W\mathbf{k})\) is negative when \(W\mathbf{k}\) matches the value: the update doubles (loss −8.00 instead of the −4.00 of one pass) and none reads back well.

With squared error and \(\eta = 1\), one step writes a chunk of well-separated keys in full; a second pass leaves \(W\) unchanged, while the dot-product loss doubles the update.

How it works

Take item 3 of the last section (key \((0.6,0.8)\), value \((5,-4)\)) and let \(W\) be the \(S\) of that section after items 1 and 2. The squared-error loss is \(\tfrac12\lVert W\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{v}\rVert^2\), with \(W\mathbf{k} = (1,2.2)\), since \(3 \times 0.6 + (-1)\times 0.8 = 1\) and \(1 \times 0.6 + 2 \times 0.8 = 2.2\). The miss is \(W\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{v} = (-4,6.2)\), the gradient of the loss with respect to \(W\) is \((W\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{k}^\top\), and a step of size \(\eta = 1\) against it adds \((4,-6.2)\,\mathbf{k}^\top\). This is the delta-rule update of the last section.

\(W\)after the chunk=\(W\)before the chunk+\(\eta\)step size×\(\sum_{t\in\text{chunk}}(\mathbf{v}_t-W\mathbf{k}_t)\,\mathbf{k}_t^\top\)a delta-rule step per token

The steps of all tokens in a chunk use the \(W\) from before the chunk and are applied together after it. A step on the dot-product loss \(-\mathbf{v}\cdot(W\mathbf{k})\) adds \(\eta\,\mathbf{v}\mathbf{k}^\top\) to \(W\), the sum update of the last section. In-Place TTT, the method of my project, uses this loss. It updates the down projection, the last matrix of an MLP block, in some blocks after a chunk of 4,096 tokens (see the Go deeper part below).

Common belief. Test-time training means the model keeps learning from all it reads, for good.

Why it fails. The fast weights start from the same trained values for all inputs, and the saved model never changes (my primer, step by step). What the model learned from one report is gone when the next input starts.

Better account. Test-time training is a temporary memory kept in weights, like a notepad wiped after a conversation, except that the rule for what to write was itself trained beforehand.

Quick quiz

Which weights change in test-time training, and when do they go back to their trained values?

Only the fast weights change (here the matrix \(W\); in In-Place TTT the down projections of selected blocks). They start again from the trained values when the next input starts.

Why is a chunk read with the weights from before its own update?

The update is applied after the chunk has been read, so a chunk cannot use its own update to predict its own tokens.

Go deeper derivation, my project, a debug tip about 4 min

Reading the figure

Press Read next chunk. The coral bracket marks the chunk just read. The matrix W is the only thing that changes. Its starting value is \(W_0\), and chunk 1 is read with \(W_0\), chunk 2 with the matrix after the first update, and so on. Then try three things. First, set the chunk to 8 tokens and the step size to 1.2 with squared error, and read the loss on the second chunk (random keys appear after token 8). It goes up from 9.25 to 14.39, because a large chunk with overlapping keys needs a smaller step. Second, switch to the dot-product loss and press Chunks read twice. The write doubles, because that loss is linear in W and has no lowest point. Third, switch back to squared error with a step size of 1, set the chunk to 4 and read the first chunk twice. The second pass leaves W unchanged, because W already fits: the keys of the first 8 tokens are at right angles, so one step of size 1 writes them in full.

From the delta rule to a gradient step

The link to the last section is a derivation. Take a loss on one pair, \(L(W) = \tfrac12\lVert W\mathbf{k} - \mathbf{v}\rVert^2\). Its slope with respect to \(W\) is \((W\mathbf{k} - \mathbf{v})\mathbf{k}^\top\), so one gradient step of size \(\eta\) is \(W \leftarrow W + \eta(\mathbf{v} - W\mathbf{k})\mathbf{k}^\top\), the delta rule. A test-time training layer (Sun and others, 2024) makes its hidden state such a model, a linear map or a small MLP. It updates the model by a step of a self-supervised loss as the sequence is read. The update can be made on a chunk (a mini-batch) of tokens at a time, which is what the chunk slider changes.

The update of a chunk

\[ W \leftarrow W - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}, \qquad \Delta W_{\text{chunk}} = \eta\sum_{t\in\text{chunk}} (\mathbf{v}_t - W\mathbf{k}_t)\,\mathbf{k}_t^\top \]

  • \(W\) is the fast weight, and \(\eta\) the step size. \(\mathbf{k}_t\) and \(\mathbf{v}_t\) are a key and a target built from token \(t\) of the input.
  • With squared error the step is the sum of the delta-rule steps of the chunk, computed with the \(W\) from before the chunk. With chunk size 1 it is the delta rule of the last section.

A chunk is read with the weights from before its own update. This also means that a chunk cannot help to predict its own tokens, so a target that looks a few tokens ahead does not leak the answer. The rule for what to write into the fast weights was itself trained beforehand, so that what is written is useful for predicting the next token.

My project

Bridge to my project. In-Place Test-Time Training, a method from ByteDance Seed (Feng and others), treats the down projection of selected MLP blocks as fast weights. It updates them chunk by chunk as the model reads, with a target built from the input. The MLP blocks are those of D5. My primer describes it for Qwen3-4B: six of the 36 blocks (layers 0, 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30), updated chunk by chunk with chunks of 4,096 tokens. The update has the form of the sum above with the dot-product loss: \(\Delta W = \eta \sum_t \hat{\mathbf{v}}_t \mathbf{h}_t^\top\). Here \(\mathbf{h}_t\) is the hidden vector the MLP computes anyway. The target \(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_t\) is built from the input by a short convolution and a projection. Generation never pauses: an update happens in the step that completes a chunk. A chunk is read with the weights from before its own update. In-Place TTT keeps the ordinary attention and its KV cache. The fast weight is an extra memory in the MLP. At MBZUAI, in Prof. Salman Khan's group, I am porting the method from text models to a Qwen vision-language model, so that it can adapt to an input after deployment. My primer builds it up from attention: see writing into a matrix, the target, the loss and the gradient, when the update runs and the KV cache. C3 shows the plainer relative of this idea, which changes the scale and shift of batch norm on a stream of photos.

The chapters on domain shift and continual learning give simpler versions of test-time training.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the loss on the chunk rises after the update, the step is too large for the chunk. Lower \(\eta\) or the chunk size. A loss that is linear in the weights, like the one In-Place TTT uses, has no lowest point, so the step size alone decides how far W moves.

Four routes side by side

Guess first. Of the four routes (full cache, sparse attention, a linear or state-space layer, test-time training), which keep a full copy of the old tokens, and which keep a summary?

A route is a way to let a model read a long text. Full attention keeps the key and value of all old tokens. Sparse attention keeps a window and a few global tokens. A linear or state-space layer keeps one matrix of fixed size, in which the items overlap. Test-time training keeps a weight matrix that gradient steps write while the model reads. Sparse attention and a linear or state-space layer give up part of a full memory to lower the cost, and they give up different parts. In-Place TTT keeps its matrix beside the ordinary attention and its cache, so it adds memory.

  1. The top row of boxes is the text and below it is what the route keeps. Press “Next route” to step through the four routes.
  2. At the start (32,768 tokens, Qwen3-4B sizes) the table gives memory per layer. Full attention needs 67,108,864 numbers, the sparse route 8,396,800, a hypothetical linear layer 131,072 and test-time training 24,903,680 beside the cache.
  3. Drag the length slider to 1,000,000: only the first row grows (the table drops tokens outside the sparse pattern).

At 32,768 tokens the full cache stores all old tokens in 67,108,864 numbers per layer, the sparse route 8,396,800, a hypothetical linear layer 131,072 and test-time training 24,903,680 beside the cache.

How it works

Take 32,768 tokens with the sizes of Qwen3-4B (8 key-value heads of 128 numbers, so a key or a value has 1,024 numbers). Full attention stores \(2 \times 32{,}768 \times 1{,}024 = 67{,}108{,}864\) numbers per layer. The sparse route, with a window \(w = 4{,}096\) and \(g = 4\) global tokens, stores \(2 \times 4{,}100 \times 1{,}024 = 8{,}396{,}800\). The fixed-size rows do not depend on \(n\). A hypothetical linear layer has 8 matrices of 128 by 128, one per key-value head, which is \(8 \times 128 \times 128 = 131{,}072\) numbers. The down projection that In-Place TTT updates (2,560 by 9,728) has 24,903,680.

\(\text{memory}\)numbers per layer=2key and value×\(n\) or \(w+g\)tokens kept×1,024\(n_{kv}\,d_{\text{head}}\)

Full attention loses no information, and its memory grows with \(n\). If the cache drops the tokens that the pattern never reads, the sparse route stops growing at \(w+g\) tokens, and the far tokens are lost. A fixed-size matrix stays the same size, and its items overlap, so it loses detail when more is stored than it can separate.

Common belief. One of the four routes is the best for a long text.

Why it fails. For a 40-minute dive, “How many hammerhead events were there?” is a summary question, for which a fixed memory may be enough. “At what second did the detector first see a milk shark?” is a lookup of one moment, for which a cache can find the key.

Better account. No route is best in general. The choice depends on what a task needs from far back, and the way to know is to test. A system for the dive can use more than one route.

Quick quiz

At 1,000,000 tokens, how many numbers per layer does the sparse route need?

\(2 \times 4{,}100 \times 1{,}024 = 8{,}396{,}800\), the same as at 32,768 tokens, because, if the cache drops the tokens that the pattern never reads, the route stops growing once the text is longer than \(w+g = 4{,}100\) tokens.

Which route would you use to find when a milk shark was first seen, and why?

A cache (full attention, or a window that still contains that moment). The answer is a lookup of one old token, and a fixed memory keeps only a summary.

Go deeper the four routes, a question about 2 min

Reading the figure

Step through the routes. The top row of boxes is the text. Below it is what a route keeps. Raise the length and watch the table. The memory of the first row grows with \(n\). The sparse route stops growing once the window is full, and the two fixed-size rows do not change.

The table uses the sizes of Qwen3-4B: 8 key-value heads of size 128. The row for linear or state-space layers is a hypothetical matrix of 128 by 128 per head, and the row for test-time training uses the down projection of Qwen3-4B. Only the full cache keeps all old tokens in full. The sparse route keeps a window and a few global tokens, and the fixed-size routes keep a sum in which the items overlap, or what an update rule wrote.

The four routes

  • Full attention. Accurate, simple, and trained the usual way. The cost is the square of the length in time and a straight line in memory.
  • Sparse attention. A window plus global or strided links. The cost grows in a straight line or as \(n\sqrt{n}\). The model is usually trained with the pattern, and details outside it are lost.
  • Linear attention and state-space models. The memory is a matrix or a state of fixed size. The cost per token does not grow. The memory is a summary, and some models mix a few full layers into a stack of such layers.
  • Test-time training. The memory is a set of weights trained as the text is read, with a rule that was itself trained beforehand. It can be added beside attention, as In-Place TTT does, or be the hidden state of a layer.

More questions

Why is a model usually trained with the route it will use?

Sparse attention changes what a token can read. A model trained with full attention gives different answers when pairs are removed: the loss of GPT-2 small rose from 1.69 to 7.84 with a window of 128. The fixed-size and trained-memory routes also change the architecture, so they are trained as well.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A causal window of \(w = 4\) over \(n = 10\) tokens computes \(w n - w(w-1)/2 = 34\) pairs. Count the keys row by row to check. Then derive the count for a window read both ways with \(h\) tokens on both sides, and compute it for \(n = 10\) and \(h = 1\).

    Hint

    The first and last \(h\) rows are shorter. Count the rows at the edge separately: row \(i\) has \(\min(i, h) + 1 + \min(n - 1 - i, h)\) keys, with \(i\) starting at 0.

  2. theory Show that attention and the rest of a layer cost the same at \(n^{*} = P_{\text{block}} / d_a - 1\). For a model with \(P_{\text{block}} \approx 12 d^2\) and \(d_a = d\), find \(n^{*}\) for \(d = 1{,}024\).

    Hint

    Divide \(n(n+1)d_a = n\,P_{\text{block}}\) by \(n\,d_a\).

  3. theory Qwen2.5-0.5B has 24 layers, 2 key-value heads of size 64 and about 0.49 billion weights. How large is its cache for 32,768 tokens in 16-bit numbers, and how does it compare with the weights?

  4. theory Two items with keys \((1,0)\) and \((0.8,0.6)\) and values \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) are written into a 2 by 2 matrix. Compute the matrix with the sum rule and with the delta rule (\(\eta = 1\)), and the read-outs for both keys. Which rule gives the smaller error for the first item?

Practice

  1. practice With the NumPy code of the mask section, count the pairs of the strided pattern for \(n = 2{,}400\) and strides \(l = 10, 49, 100\). Find the stride that gives the fewest pairs, and compare it with \(\sqrt{n/2}\).

    Hint

    Loop over \(l\) from 2 to 200 and keep the smallest count. The count is about \(n\,l + n^2/(2l)\).

  2. practice Use the function kv_bytes to size the cache of Qwen3-4B for the dive log in two formats: as sentences (109,699 tokens) and as table rows (72,704 tokens). How many of the two fit in 16 GB after the weights?

  3. practice Write window attention that only computes the allowed pairs (a loop or a banded matrix). Compare its run time with the masked full version for \(n = 2{,}000\) and \(w = 64\), and check that the outputs agree.

    Hint

    For token \(t\), slice k[max(0, t-w+1):t+1] and v in the same way. Use time.perf_counter() around both versions.

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam must keep a running memory of a 40-minute dive on a small computer with 8 GB of memory. Which route, or which mix of routes, would you choose, and what would you measure before deciding? Think about what questions the crew will ask.

  2. open A model has a window of 128,000 tokens. Design a test, using the made-up dive log, to find out whether it uses a detection buried in the middle as well as one at the start or the end. What would you vary, what would you keep fixed, and what result would convince you?

  3. open A cache keeps the user's text in memory until the conversation ends. Fast weights keep a summary of it, in numbers, until the input ends. List one situation where the second is better for the user and one where it is worse.

Come back later

(D4, D5) Why can the KV cache store keys and values once and reuse them, and why does that mean a sliding window can also drop old ones?

Earlier tokens never read later ones, so their keys and values never change (the causal mask). With a window, tokens older than \(w\) are never read again by later queries, so their keys and values can be deleted from the cache.

(C3, B7) In C3 a test-time loop updated 96 of 20,874 numbers on a stream of photos, and In-Place TTT updates the down projections of six blocks. What do both leave fixed, and why is that a good idea?

Both leave most of the model fixed and update a small set of weights chosen in advance. The small set keeps the update cheap and limits how far the model can drift from what it learned, which is the worry about forgetting in B7.

(D1, D4) A Hindi report costs 117 tokens and its English meaning 23. How many times as many causal pairs does the Hindi report have?

\(117 \times 118 / 2 = 6{,}903\) against \(23 \times 24 / 2 = 276\), which is 25 times as many.
